items.title: World Toilet Day: Sanitation must become an affordable investment for every household
items.description: The 2025–2026 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey shows that 76 per cent of households have access to improved sanitation facilities.
content: Access to a safe toilet is fundamental to public health, dignity and well-being. While Kenya has made progress in expanding access to improved sanitation, disparities in household circumstances, infrastructure and affordability mean that more needs to be done to extend these gains to every community.

The 2025–2026 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey shows that 76 per cent of households have access to improved sanitation facilities. However, the proportion stands at 63 per cent in rural areas, compared with 93 per cent in urban areas. The survey also indicates that 45 per cent of the population has access to at least basic sanitation services, while 7.4 per cent still practise open defecation.

These findings underscore the importance of sustaining investments in sanitation while addressing the different needs of households. Access to an improved toilet is an important step, but safely managed sanitation also requires hygienic and durable facilities supported by appropriate waste containment and management systems.

The Ministry of Health’s Costed National Sanitation and Hygiene Roadmap 2023–2030 provides an indication of the investment required. It estimates that a basic G1 sanitation unit, designed to provide a clean and flyproof toilet, costs between KES 10,000 and KES 12,000 in hardware, depending on county conditions. A more durable individual G2 toilet with safe waste containment costs between KES 25,000 and KES 30,000.

items.title: End of an era? Kenya’s 'established' politicians face relevance test before 2027
Sifuna breaks silence on Linda Mwananchi rift
items.description: Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna yesterday broke his silence over deepening divisions within the Linda Mwananchi Movement, disputing claims by Embakasi East MP Babu Owino that he had reneged on a power-sharing agreement and directly challenging colleagues who have questioned his fitness to lead the coalition's political party ahead of the 2027 General Election.
content: Kenya’s opposition coalition fractures over party leadership and power-sharing as the 2027 presidential race takes shape.

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna yesterday broke his silence over deepening divisions within the Linda Mwananchi Movement, disputing claims by Embakasi East MP Babu Owino that he had reneged on a power-sharing agreement and directly challenging colleagues who have questioned his fitness to lead the coalition’s political party ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Speaking in an interview on Royal Media radio stations — Citizen Radio, Mulembé, Sulwe and Vuka FM — Sifuna offered a detailed and pointed account of how the movement’s leadership arrangements were negotiated, how they unravelled, and why he believes government interference rather than personal betrayal lies at the root of the coalition’s current troubles. The intervention was significant not simply as a rebuttal but as a signal: Sifuna is not stepping aside, and Linda Mwananchi, whatever its internal tensions, is not dissolving without a fight.

The dispute traces back to the formation of a unified opposition political vehicle following the exit of several leaders from ODM. Sifuna recounted how the group, now homeless politically, began searching for a new party structure. “We were looking for a new house to be able to ensure that all of us could take shelter in there,” he said. Five leaders put forward their respective parties for consideration — Babu Owino, Caroli Omondi, Godfrey Osotsi, George Natembeya and Caleb Amisi. A sub-committee was established to submit party documents for legal evaluation, assessing each outfit’s registration status, structure, compliance and ownership before recommending which one was best placed to serve as the coalition’s common vehicle.

The group eventually settled on the Equitable Party. Omondi abandoned his own party to join the arrangement, as did former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza and Mavoko MP Patrick Makau. Sifuna was then designated party leader and presidential candidate — a decision he maintains was reached collectively and transparently. His challenge to those now questioning that outcome was blunt: “Is it possible you trust me to be president of the country but you cannot trust me to be party leader of a party?” The logic, as he framed it, was straightforward. A coalition willing to back him for the highest office in Kenya but unwilling to trust him with party leadership had a credibility problem — and that problem did not belong to him.

Babu’s account differs. The Embakasi East MP, who has since declared his candidacy for the Nairobi governorship, stated publicly that the original agreement was for Sifuna to be the presidential candidate while he took the position of party leader. “Initially, we had agreed with Sifuna and other members that the moment we get the party out, Sifuna would be the presidential candidate and I would be the party leader. But things changed. I also don’t know how things changed,” Babu said. It is a claim Sifuna does not directly deny so much as contextualise — arguing that the arrangements evolved through collective decision-making rather than unilateral action on his part.

The complication, Sifuna explained, arose when some members raised concerns about the political practicalities of operating under a single party in their home regions. Leaders from Luo Nyanza, in particular, argued that retaining their own parties gave them greater capacity to defend their electoral strongholds and secure parliamentary seats. The group accommodated that position. “We agreed. If you must be party leader so people enter your party, it’s okay,” Sifuna said. The concession, in his telling, was an act of pragmatism — not weakness. But it left the coalition with a structure that is simultaneously unified in purpose and fractured in form.

Sifuna was careful to distinguish between political disagreements and personal estrangement. He insisted that neither Babu, Orengo nor PM Party leader Caleb Amisi had personally confronted him with accusations of betrayal. “When you talk about rumours, especially these rumours I see on social media, Babu himself or Orengo or Caleb hasn’t said that Sifuna has wronged him anywhere,” he said. The charge of betrayal, in his view, is being amplified externally — and he placed that amplification squarely at the door of the government. He accused state actors of deliberately working to fracture the opposition, arguing that the narrative of internal collapse serves those who fear a united front against President William Ruto in 2027.

Whether that explanation fully accounts for the coalition’s difficulties is debatable. Amisi’s warning — that if Sifuna is not at the opposition flagbearer table, “we will break that table” — does not read as the language of a movement at ease with itself. Orengo’s decision to shift focus to building his own Liberal Democratic Party, and Babu’s pivot to the Nairobi governorship race, suggest that the centrifugal forces within Linda Mwananchi are real and not entirely manufactured from outside.

What is clear is that the opposition’s structural challenge — how to build a coalition broad enough to defeat Ruto while keeping together leaders with competing ambitions, regional constituencies and rival political vehicles — remains unresolved. Sifuna disclosed that the group has held more than 100 meetings in pursuit of a unified party arrangement, without achieving it. “The hope that Kenyans have placed in Linda Mwananchi does not allow me to have side shows,” he said. It was part warning to colleagues, part reassurance to supporters — and a reminder that the clock is running.

With August 2027 approaching and a sitting president already mobilising his grassroots machinery, Kenya’s opposition cannot afford the luxury of prolonged internal theatre. The Linda Mwananchi rift may yet be resolved — Sifuna’s networks span Western Kenya and beyond, and the coalition retains genuine depth. But unity forged in meeting rooms and radio interviews is not the same as unity demonstrated at the ballot box. For now, the movement’s leaders are still arguing about the table. The election will come regardless.

items.title: Canada to Offer 5,500 Slots to Foreign Workers by Making Rural Programme Permanent
items.description: Canada makes the Rural Community Immigration Programme permanent, with 5,500 annual places across 14 communities to tackle persistent rural labour shortages.
content: Elijah Ntongai is an experienced editor at TUKO.co.ke, with more than four years in financial, business, labour and technology reporting. His work provides valuable insights into Kenyan, African, and global trends.
Canada has permanently established a rural immigration pathway designed to help smaller communities address long-standing workforce shortages, the federal government announced on November 9, 2026.

Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab made the announcement in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, confirming that the Rural Community Immigration Pilot has been converted into a permanent programme under the country's 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan.
UK Embassy Kenya announces deadline to apply for 2027 fully funded Commonwealth scholarships

The employer- and community-led initiative is structured around local partnerships between businesses and community organisations, with the aim of connecting newcomers and their families to the support networks necessary for long-term settlement.
The government plans to retain the 14 communities currently participating in the pilot, with further expansion to additional communities planned at a later stage.
For the 2027 admissions cycle, the government has set a target of 5,500 spaces under the now-permanent Rural Community Immigration Programme.
The initiative traces its roots to the Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot, which ran from 2019 to 2024 and saw more than 2,800 employers participate.
Over 12,500 candidates and their families were admitted to rural and smaller communities through that pilot.
The current Rural Community Immigration Pilot, launched in 2025, has already shown early impact.
Canada seeks welders and 25 other priority jobs to apply and live in its villages
Between January 2025 and August 2026, participating communities vetted and designated more than 1,950 trusted employers facing persistent labour shortages.
Those employers issued over 4,700 job offers and community recommendations, with newcomers helping to fill vacancies in sectors including health care, education, and sales and services.
Jason Guidry, Chief Executive Officer of Pictou County Partnership, said the permanent status of the programme would give rural regions greater certainty when planning for workforce needs.

Amber Manning, Human Resources Manager at WearWell Garments Limited, a Pictou County manufacturer established in 1978, highlighted the practical value of immigration pathways for businesses struggling to find skilled workers locally.
Canada announces jobs for Kenyans and other foreigners, lists 7 in-demand categories

The programme sits alongside other permanent residence pathways, including the Provincial Nominee Programme and federal economic programmes managed through Express Entry, as well as various temporary immigration routes available to employers across Canada.
In other news, the US Department of State clarified the purposes of its three main passport application forms , warning that submitting the wrong one could delay processing.

Form DS-11 is for first-time applicants, children under 16 and individuals who do not qualify for renewal, while DS-82 is reserved for eligible passport renewals by mail or through the online service.
Form DS-5504 is used to correct or update passport information, change a name or replace a passport originally issued with limited validity.

Applicants can use the State Department's online form guide and fee calculator to identify the correct application, with those applying from outside the US advised to check their nearest American embassy or consulate for country-specific instructions.

Kenya Airways has advertised three senior permanent positions at its Nairobi headquarters as part of its ongoing strategic recovery and growth agenda, with applications closing in late November 2026.

The national carrier is recruiting for a Head of KQ Academy, a Head of Fleet Development, and a Head of Employee Relations, all of which carry direct reporting lines to the airline's most senior executives.

The Head of KQ Academy will serve as the principal architect of the airline's enterprise learning strategy and as the Accountable Manager of its Approved Training Organisation (ATO), which operates under the oversight of the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) and in accordance with ICAO standards.
The role reports to the Chief People Officer and carries responsibility for both regulatory and commercial training, including revenue-generating programmes offered to external aviation clients.

Candidates must hold a bachelor's degree in a relevant discipline and bring at least 10 years of learning and development experience, with a minimum of five years in a senior leadership role. The position closes on November 25, 2026.
The Head of Fleet Development is accountable for managing Kenya Airways' aircraft fleet across the full lifecycle, from acquisition and entry into service through to disposal and redelivery.

The minimum requirement is 10 years of progressive industry experience, with at least seven years directly relevant to fleet management or aircraft transactions. A university degree in engineering, finance, or law is mandatory. The application deadline is November 24, 2026.

The Head of Employee Relations will oversee the employment relationship across a workforce of more than 4,500 staff operating in over 30 countries.

The role carries responsibility for collective bargaining with multiple trade unions, compliance with Kenyan employment legislation, and the management of employment litigation before the Employment and Labour Relations Court.

Candidates must hold a bachelor's degree in human resources, law, or a related field, along with a mandatory professional HR certification such as CHRP (K) from the Institute of Human Resource Management (IHRM) Kenya.
A minimum of 12 years of HR experience is required, with at least seven years in a senior employee relations leadership capacity. The position closes on November 25, 2026.
All three roles are based at Kenya Airways headquarters in Nairobi. The airline specifies that only candidates with the right to live and work in Kenya will be considered.
Interested applicants are required to submit their curriculum vitae through the Kenya Airways careers portal.

Opportunities are available across nine departments, including Finance, Research, Banking and Payment Services, Communications, Human Resources, Legal Services, Internal Audit, General Services and Information Technology.

content: Equity Bank has announced multiple career opportunities for professionals interested in joining its operations in Kenya and supporting programmes extending across different markets. The latest recruitment drive features 18 vacancies covering banking, financial crime compliance, data and analytics, project management, climate adaptation finance, monitoring and evaluation, gender and social inclusion, youth banking and the creative economy.

The opportunities provide openings for professionals at different management and specialist levels. Several positions are focused on strengthening the Bank’s regulatory compliance and financial crime management framework, including transaction monitoring, KYC advisory, AML policies, regulatory change and data-driven compliance testing.

Other vacancies support the Africa Rural Climate Adaptation Finance Mechanism (ARCAFIM), including positions concerned with programme coordination, climate adaptation banking, gender and social inclusion, and monitoring and evaluation. Equity Bank is also recruiting professionals to support its Youth Banking and Creative Economy portfolios.

Equity Bank Kenya Limited describes itself as a technology-driven financial services institution whose operations include banking, insurance, payments, technology, investment and social impact. Its broader strategy focuses on financial inclusion, economic empowerment, innovation and sustainable development.

Applicants should carefully review the requirements attached to their preferred position before submitting an application. Closing dates vary, with some of the earliest vacancies closing on November 24, 2026.
Below are the 18 Equity Bank job vacancies currently advertised.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: December 17, 2026

Equity Bank is recruiting a Regional Coordinator for its operations in Kenya. The position provides an opportunity for a professional interested in supporting regional-level coordination and implementation.

As a coordination position, the successful candidate will operate within the structures established by the Bank for the relevant programme or business area and support effective delivery across the assigned region.

Candidates interested in this position should refer to the official Equity Bank vacancy notice for the complete job description, responsibilities and eligibility requirements before applying. This is particularly important because the vacancy information supplied for this listing does not contain the full detailed job description.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 27, 2026

The Senior AML Manager – Transaction Monitoring will strengthen the effectiveness of Equity Bank’s risk-based Anti-Money Laundering, Counter Financing of Terrorism and Counter Proliferation Financing transaction-monitoring framework.

The position provides Second Line governance over transaction-monitoring coverage, scenario development and calibration, alert quality and data integrity. It also supports escalation of suspicious activity to the Money Laundering Reporting Officer.
The role also maintains the Bank’s documented transaction-monitoring framework and supports regulatory inspections, independent reviews and audits.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 27, 2026
The Manager – Transaction Monitoring will support the assessment and strengthening of Equity Bank’s risk-based AML/CFT/CPF transaction-monitoring controls.
The position focuses on monitoring coverage, detection scenarios, alert-management standards, data completeness and escalation of potentially suspicious activity.
The position also supports regulatory inspections, independent reviews and audits involving transaction-monitoring controls.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 27, 2026
The Manager – Testing (Data & Analytics) will plan and execute independent, data-driven Second Line testing of financial crime and regulatory controls.
The role uses analytics and data testing to assess controls, identify exceptions and document evidence-based findings and their root causes.
The role is particularly focused on producing testing that is documented, repeatable and capable of independent review.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026

The Senior Manager – Testing (Data & Analytics) will independently evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of regulatory and financial crime controls using data-driven Second Line testing methodologies.
The position leads population-based testing, analytics and continuous monitoring while providing management and Board committees with information about control effectiveness.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026

This position is responsible for proactive identification, interpretation, governance and oversight of regulatory changes, compliance policies, standards and regulatory obligations affecting the Bank.
The Senior Compliance Manager will help translate regulatory requirements into clear policies, accountable ownership and effective controls.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Senior Manager – KYC Advisory will provide specialist risk-based advice concerning Know Your Customer, Customer Due Diligence and Enhanced Due Diligence requirements.
The position provides independent challenge and oversight of financial-crime risks associated with customers and complex relationships.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Manager – Regulatory Change, AML Policies & Standards will support the identification and interpretation of AML/CFT/CPF regulatory developments.
The role is also responsible for maintaining relevant policies, standards and the Bank’s regulatory-obligations register.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Manager – Project Management Office will coordinate governance, planning, monitoring and reporting for complex regulatory-remediation and compliance-transformation programmes.
The position is intended to ensure that commitments made to regulators are properly tracked and delivered while risks and delays are escalated through appropriate governance structures.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Manager – AML & KYC Advisory will provide risk-based AML/CFT/CPF and KYC advisory opinions concerning customer onboarding, retention and higher-risk customer relationships.
The role provides independent review and challenge while ensuring that advisory decisions are appropriately documented.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Gender & Social Inclusion Coordinator will lead the technical-assistance and inclusion agenda under ARCAFIM.

The role focuses on enabling small-scale rural producers and small and medium-sized agribusinesses to access and sustainably benefit from climate-responsive financing, with particular attention to women, youth, low-income rural producers and underserved communities.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026

The Climate Change Adaptation Banking Coordinator will lead the design, rollout and performance management of ARCAFIM’s climate-change-adaptation lending component across participating Equity Bank Group subsidiaries.
The position will help expand climate-resilient financing for small-scale rural producers and value-chain actors, including women and young people.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Monitoring & Evaluation Officer will lead the design and operation of ARCAFIM’s monitoring, evaluation and learning framework.
The position will provide evidence concerning programme lending, technical assistance and outcomes while supporting reporting to Equity Bank management and IFAD.
The official vacancy also identifies results-based management, survey design, data analysis, digital M&E tools and data-quality assurance as important areas for the position.
Location: Multiple Locations Closing Date: November 26, 2026
The Programme Coordinator will lead planning, coordination and delivery of ARCAFIM across participating Equity Bank entities.
The role provides strategic and operational oversight of the Programme Management Unit while coordinating climate-change-adaptation financing and capacity-building activities.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 24, 2026

The Relationship Manager – Youth Banking will lead growth and development of Equity Bank’s youth portfolio by expanding customer acquisition, strengthening banking relationships and encouraging digital adoption.
The role will also develop partnerships across youth-focused ecosystems and support growth in deposits, responsible lending and revenue.
Location: Multiple Locations Closing Date: November 24, 2026
Equity Bank is seeking a Data & Innovation Manager to support its Youth Banking business.
The position sits within an area of the Bank that uses technology, data and innovation to expand financial inclusion and develop financial solutions for younger customers.

The successful candidate will work within the Bank’s Youth Banking framework and contribute to the use of data and innovation in supporting customer growth, engagement and the continued development of youth-focused financial services.

Applicants should review the complete official Equity Bank vacancy notice for the detailed duties, experience requirements, academic requirements and other conditions attached to this particular position, as the vacancy information supplied for this article does not contain the complete job description.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 24, 2026
The Business Development Manager – Youth Banking will lead development and management of strategic partnerships that increase Equity Bank’s reach within the youth market.
The position will build youth-focused ecosystems across educational institutions, employers, technology hubs, creative industries and other strategic partners.
Location: Kenya Closing Date: November 24, 2026

The Business Development Manager/Specialist – Creative Economy will support commercial growth within the creative economy by translating Equity Bank’s strategy into financial propositions, partnerships and business opportunities.
The position focuses on creators, artists, athletes, gig workers and digital entrepreneurs and seeks to expand the Bank’s participation in these emerging economic segments.
Applicants should note that the 18 vacancies do not share a single closing date.
Applicants are encouraged to submit their applications before the relevant closing date rather than waiting until the final day.

Interested candidates should access the official Equity Bank recruitment portal, select the position that matches their professional background and carefully read the complete vacancy notice before beginning an application.
Candidates should ensure that information submitted during the recruitment process is accurate and that all documents requested through the recruitment portal are provided in the required format.

Because each vacancy has its own responsibilities and eligibility requirements, applicants should rely on the requirements stated in the individual official job advertisement rather than assuming that requirements for one Equity Bank position apply to another.
Applications for these vacancies are being handled online through Equity Bank’s recruitment system.

items.title: Kenya Construction Regulator Flags Inspection Gaps After 72 Collapses
items.description: Kenya's National Construction Authority covers only 27 counties with five Nairobi inspectors after 72 building collapses in three years, amid heavy rains.
content: Kenya's National Construction Authority covers only 27 counties with five Nairobi inspectors after 72 building collapses in three years, amid heavy rains.

Kenya's National Construction Authority has warned that severe underfunding leaves it operating in only 27 of the country's 47 counties, even after 72 buildings collapsed nationwide over the past three years.

According to a November 19, 2026 Citizen TV report and a November 20 Kenyans.co.ke update, the regulator faces acute staffing constraints as seasonal heavy rainfall heightens structural risks across active construction zones. In Nairobi, the epicentre of Kenya's high-rise development boom, only five NCA inspection officers are tasked with overseeing thousands of ongoing projects.

The disclosure exposes a central contradiction in Kenya's built environment: while the state replaced a 56-year-old colonial building order in February 2025 with the National Building Code, 2024, front-line capacity to verify whether developers follow those rules has fallen far behind the pace of urban construction.

Leaving 20 Kenyan counties without an NCA operational footprint forces regulators to stretch sparse teams across wide regions or rely on reactive checks after failures occur. With only five inspectors assigned to Nairobi's entire construction pipeline, routine site verification across excavation, foundation curing, concrete mixing, and multi-storey framing becomes physically impossible at scale.

The human stakes of inspection gaps were underscored in Eastleigh, Nairobi, where an 18-storey building collapsed in October 2026. On November 5, the fourteenth day of search and rescue operations, Citizen TV reported that teams recovered six additional bodies, bringing the confirmed death toll to eight while five people remained unaccounted for and families waited for answers.

Increased rainfall across Kenya adds immediate physical stress to compromised structures. Waterlogged soils reduce bearing capacity under shallow or poorly engineered foundations, while unsealed concrete slabs and inadequate drainage accelerate structural degradation on stalled or hurried sites.

Preventing structural failures requires coordination across multiple laws and institutions rather than a single agency acting alone. Under Kenya's statutory framework, responsibility is divided between county governments and national regulators at distinct stages of a project's life cycle.

In practice, that split creates dangerous seams. County governments issue initial development permissions and approve architectural and structural plans under the Physical and Land Use Planning Act. The NCA, established under Act No. 41 of 2011, registers contractors, accredits site supervisors and skilled workers, registers projects, and monitors compliance on active sites.

When county plan-vetting, NCA site registration, and physical inspections fail to align, unauthorised floors, unverified design changes, or unapproved occupancy can persist undetected until a structure fails. Published in Kenya Gazette No.

28 on March 1, 2024 and commenced on February 20, 2025, the National Building Code, 2024 replaced the 1968 Local Government Building Order with updated rules on structural design, fire protection, electrical installations, occupancy certification, and enforcement. Yet updated legal standards cannot inspect concrete pours on their own.

Even when inspectors flag violations, the gap between legal authority and sustained enforcement remains wide across fast-growing neighbourhoods. Developers face intense commercial pressure to finish multi-storey residential blocks quickly and occupy ground floors before upper levels or certification procedures are complete.

Public records reviewed from the November 19 and November 20 briefings do not disclose the exact size of the NCA's current funding shortfall in shillings, nor has the regulator published a county-by-county breakdown identifying where the 72 collapses occurred or how many resulted in criminal convictions.

Under the National Construction Authority Act, contractors, site supervisors, and skilled construction workers must hold accreditation, and ongoing projects must be registered before works proceed. However, without enough county offices or inspectors to verify compliance on the ground, registration risks remaining a paper formality rather than an active safety filter.

For prospective tenants, buyers, and lenders, the practical baseline is clear: verifying both county development approvals and NCA project registration before committing money remains essential, yet self-checks cannot substitute for state inspections. Until Kenya matches its 2024 Building Code with funded inspectors across all 47 counties, heavy rains and rapid high-rise construction will continue to test weak links in the regulatory chain.

items.title: Edna Karijo Wins Women In Tech Leadership Award At Africa Tech Festival 2026
items.description: Kenya’s Edna Karijo has won the Women in Tech Leadership Award at the Africa Tech Festival Awards 2026
content: Edna Karijo, Associate Director at eMobilis Technology Training Institute, has won the Women in Tech Leadership Award at the Africa Tech Festival Awards 2026. The winners were announced at a gala evening in Cape Town on 18 November, during the 2026 edition of Africa Tech Festival.

The award recognises women who have shown innovation, excellence and leadership in technology across the continent. Edna was shortlisted alongside Majda Lahlou Kassi of Ericsson and Shireen Powell of Project Isizwe.

Karijo leads digital skilling and inclusion work at eMobilis where she has led transformative programmes including Google’s Digital Skills for Africa, Ajira Digital Program and the Norwegian Refugee Council’s area-based livelihoods digital skills initiative. She is also a co-author of She Leads , a book of lessons from women leaders. She was also among the 2025 CIO Africa’s Top 45 Most Influential Women In Digital Transformation.

“This recognition represents far more than a personal achievement,” said Edna Karijo. “It has been a journey of dedicating many years to advocating for access to digital skills, digital inclusion, empowering communities, and creating opportunities for youth, young women, and underserved populations to benefit from technology. All this was made possible through the work at eMobilis Mobile Technology Institute and Internet Society Kenya.”

Edna also congratulated the other winners and thanked the Africa Tech Festival organisers and judges, as well as her family, colleagues, partners and networks. “This recognition belongs to all of us,” she said.

David Monaghan, Vice-President of Africa Tech Festival, said the quality of this year’s entries reflects the depth of Africa’s technology ecosystem, from multinationals to start-ups building impactful platforms.
